newsitem.title: GERMANY: Luxembourg sees "significant" number at EMU start.
newsitem.headline: Luxembourg sees "significant" number at EMU start.

text.p: Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker said on Thursday he thought a "significant" number of countries would meet the entry criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1997.

Juncker also said he was sure an Employment Chapter would be included in the Maastricht II treaty to be discussed at a European Union summit in Amsterdam next week, and stressed the need for leaders to sign Europe's planned stability pact there.

The new Socialist-led Franch government won German support for an employment chapter after it stunned Bonn on Monday by asking for a delay to study the stability pact, a code of fiscal discipline championed by Germany.

"I am sure that there will be a jobs chapter in Maastricht II, but one needs more than a bit of text to create jobs," Juncker told a business conference hosted by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats in Bonn.

Juncker, whose country takes over the rotating EU presidency next month, said a stability pact was necessary and said sticking to strict fiscal discipline did not go against the demands of the new French government to boost employment.

"There is no contradiction between good fiscal policy and a serious labour market policy," he said, adding that the best way to tackle mass unemployment was through stability and low inflation and not "overblown spending policies".

EU heads of state agreed the outlines of a stability pact, aimed at ensuring fiscal discipline after the start of the EMU, in Dublin in December. But France wants to delay ratifying the treaty, saying it wants more stress on growth and employment.
Juncker also said EMU entry criteria -- which many nations are struggling to fulfil precisely -- should be interpreted in terms of trend and not seen as inflexible targets.

The budget deficit criterion laid out in the Maastricht Treaty, which requires would-be members to limit deficits to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997, should be read as three percent, not 3.0 percent, he said.
"The three in the (Maastricht Treaty) should be interpreted in terms of trend," Juncker said.

But he said he understood why German Finance Minister Theo Waigel had stuck firmly to interpreting the goal as exactly 3.0 percent. "If Theo Waigel had said 3.8 (percent) was also okay, countries would never have made the strict effort," he said.

Juncker also said that a report from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) released on Thursday, which contained forecasts for fiscal and economic convergence in Europe in 1997, should not be overemphasised.
The report forecast that Germany, France and Italy would achieve budget deficits of 3.2 percent of GDP in 1997.
"We will have a significant number of countries who have met the convergence criteria by the end of 1997," he said.
Both Germany and France should meet EMU entry rules this year, Juncker said, adding that Italy, too, would make the grade if it did not let up on convergence efforts.

He praised Spain and Italy for their efforts to meet the EMU criteria. Contrary to the views of some, Spain and Italy had made much greater efforts to meet the EMU goals than others in Europe, he said.

Juncker went on say that the European Central Bank (ECB), which is officially due to take over the operations of the European Monetary Institute when the euro currency starts in 1999, must be a fully independent body.

"The independence of the future ECB must not be interfered with," said Juncker, echoing Bonn's rejection of a French proposal for an "economic government" as a political counterweight to the future ECB.
